title: Job 1:13–22
context: On a day when Job’s sons and daughters are eating and drinking in their oldest brother’s house, four messengers arrive in turn. The Sabeans take the oxen and donkeys and kill the servants; “The fire of God” falls from the sky on the sheep and the servants; the Chaldeans take the camels and kill the servants; a great wind from the wilderness brings down the house, and the young people in it are dead. Each time, one servant alone has escaped to tell Job. The narrator then tells how Job tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground, and worships. Job himself says, “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb, and naked will I return there. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Blessed be the LORD’s name.” The narrator closes, “In all this, Job didn’t sin, nor charge God with wrongdoing.” The deaths and the losses should be told with pastoral restraint, without graphic expansion. “The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away” is shared ground about Job’s confession, not a new box on providence. The permission-and-decree question already named at 1:12 belongs in the regular notes on 1:21 as well, and should again point to Judges 9:23 and to 2 Samuel 24:1 and 1 Chronicles 21:1, not to a new keyContrast. Shared ground remains: God is not the author of evil; Satan has acted only within the limit set in 1:12; Job is not charged with sin. The speakers are the messengers, Job, and the narrator.

verses.text: It fell on a day when his sons and his daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother’s house,
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator resumes on earth: it fell on a day when his sons and his daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother’s house. The feast of 1:4 is the scene again. The heavenly permission of 1:12 is already given; what follows will fall on that day. The verse itself only locates the children at the meal.

Arminian readers take the gathering as a real family day, brothers and sisters at table, told without foreshadowing cruelty in the meal itself.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the scene as the narrator places it, the same house and the same children, now the setting of the last report.

Both traditions move into the losses with restraint, and they invent no contrast over the feast.

verses.text: that a messenger came to Job, and said, “The oxen were plowing, and the donkeys feeding beside them,
verses.arminianNotes:
A messenger comes to Job and begins, “The oxen were plowing, and the donkeys feeding beside them,” The report opens with ordinary work, the yoke of oxen and the donkeys of 1:3 at their tasks. The speaker is the first servant who has escaped.

Arminian readers take the detail as a historical report of the moment before the raid, work in the field as it was being done.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear an ordinary scene interrupted, the livestock of Job’s greatness still at work when the first blow falls.

Both traditions let the messenger speak, and they do not decorate the coming violence beyond his words.

verses.text: and the Sabeans attacked, and took them away. Yes, they have killed the servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The same messenger continues: the Sabeans attacked, took the animals, “killed the servants with the edge of the sword,” and “I alone have escaped to tell you.” The first loss is by human raid. It falls within the power granted in 1:12, and the killing is not lingered on here. Sabeans are named and not further identified beyond a raiding people.

Arminian readers take the raid as a real human crime, permitted under the bound already set, not authored by God as evil.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also ascribe the violence to the Sabeans as its agents, under the heavenly limit already given, without making God the author of the sword.

Both traditions report the first stroke with restraint, and they keep the shared ground already stated at 1:12.

verses.text: While he was still speaking, another also came and said, “The fire of God has fallen from the sky, and has burned up the sheep and the servants, and consumed them, and I alone have escaped to tell you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
While the first is still speaking, another comes: “The fire of God has fallen from the sky, and has burned up the sheep and the servants, and consumed them, and I alone have escaped to tell you.” The messenger calls it “The fire of God” The phrase is his wording, often taken as lightning or a descending fire, but the verse does not explain the means, and it is not settled here. The second stroke also falls under 1:12, still with one survivor to tell it, and should be told without graphic addition.

Arminian readers keep the wording as the messenger’s, a disaster from the sky, within the permission already given, not a proof that God is the author of evil.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave “The fire of God” as the report given, under the LORD’s governing limit, without turning the name into a claim that God does wickedness.

Both traditions refuse to press the phrase beyond the message, and they invent no new contrast over it.

verses.text: While he was still speaking, another also came and said, “The Chaldeans made three bands, and swept down on the camels, and have taken them away, yes, and killed the servants with the edge of the sword; and I alone have escaped to tell you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
A third messenger tells of the Chaldeans, who “made three bands, and swept down on the camels, and have taken them away, yes, and killed the servants with the edge of the sword”. Again one alone has escaped. The pattern is the same: a human raid, a slaughter mentioned and not described at length, a single witness. Chaldeans are named as the attackers; no later empire is built into this line.

Arminian readers take the three bands as a real assault on the camels, another human agency within the same bound.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the Chaldeans as the secondary agents of this stroke, under the limit of 1:12, with the same restraint in the telling.

Both traditions report the third message as the narrator does, and they do not linger on the sword.

verses.text: While he was still speaking, there came also another, and said, “Your sons and your daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother’s house,
verses.arminianNotes:
While he is still speaking, another comes and says that Job’s sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother’s house. The last report begins by returning to the scene of 1:13, now addressed to Job as his sons and his daughters. Pastoral restraint is needed as the next verse completes the news.

Arminian readers take the opening as a truthful locating of the children, still at the feast, before the blow is named.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear the messenger’s first sentence as a return to the family meal, the dearest loss now about to be told.

Both traditions refuse to rush past the children, and they refuse to expand the scene beyond the report.

verses.text: and behold, there came a great wind from the wilderness, and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell on the young men, and they are dead. I alone have escaped to tell you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The messenger continues: “there came a great wind from the wilderness, and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell on the young men, and they are dead. I alone have escaped to tell you.” A wind from the wilderness brings the house down, and the children who were in it are dead. The verse should be left to say that, without graphic expansion. 1:18 has already named sons and daughters; this line says the young men are dead. The disaster takes the children in the house. The stroke is the last and the heaviest, still within the 1:12 limit, which had withheld only a hand on Job himself.

Arminian readers receive the news as the narrator and the messenger give it, a real death of Job’s children, permitted, not charged to Job as sin, and not authored by God as evil.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also tell the wind, the fallen house, and the deaths with restraint, under God’s governing bound, without making God the author of the evil, and without blaming Job.

Both traditions hold this loss as the heart of the chapter’s grief, and they invent no contrast over the wording “young men”

verses.text: Then Job arose, and tore his robe, and shaved his head, and fell down on the ground, and worshiped.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then Job arose, and tore his robe, and shaved his head, and fell down on the ground, and worshiped.” The narrator describes mourning and worship together: the torn robe, the shaved head, the fall to the ground, and worship. The speaker of the next verse will be Job; this verse is the narrator’s account of his first act after the news.

Arminian readers take the gestures as a real, whole response, grief and worship in one rising, not a denial of the loss.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see Job’s first movement as worship in mourning, the servant of 1:8 still turned toward God when everything named in 1:2–3 has been taken.

Both traditions leave the verse as the narrator tells it, and they do not hurry past the mourning to the words.

verses.text: He said, “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb, and naked will I return there. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Blessed be the LORD’s name.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Job says, “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb, and naked will I return there. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Blessed be the LORD’s name.” The speaker is Job. The confession is shared ground: he blesses the LORD’s name and ascribes both the giving and the taking to the LORD. It is not a new keyContrast on providence. How the taking relates to the Sabeans, the fire, the Chaldeans, and the wind may be described in the same terms already used at 1:12. Arminian readers typically hear Job naming the LORD who gave and who permitted the taking, without making God the author of the evil acts. Reformed readers typically hear Job naming the LORD’s sovereign hand in the taking as well as in the gift, while still denying that God is the author of sin, in line with Judges 9:23 and the census notes at 2 Samuel 24:1 and 1 Chronicles 21:1. The words “return there” are often taken of a return to the earth, not a literal return to the womb; the phrase should not be pressed beyond Job’s meaning of going back empty.

Arminian readers therefore receive the blessing as Job’s genuine worship in loss, a confession of the Giver, not a claim that God does wickedness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers receive the same words as Job’s true ascription: the LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away, and the name is blessed.

Both traditions stand with the confession, keep the existing box at Judges 9:23 in view rather than adding one, and agree that Job is not here charging God with wrong.

verses.text: In all this, Job didn’t sin, nor charge God with wrongdoing.
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator closes, “In all this, Job didn’t sin, nor charge God with wrongdoing.” The verdict is the book’s, not a friend’s and not Satan’s. In all that has been told, Job has neither sinned nor charged God with wrong. That judgment is shared ground, and it will be echoed, with slightly different wording, at 2:10. The test of 1:11 has not produced the renouncing Satan predicted.

Arminian readers take the narrator’s word as a true acquittal: Job’s worship and his confession have not crossed into sin or into an accusation against God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also receive the closing line as the book’s own measure of this first trial. Job has not sinned, and he has not charged God with wrongdoing.

Both traditions keep that verdict explicit, the third piece of the shared ground already named: God is not the author of evil; Satan has acted only within the limit; Job is not charged with sin.
